title: Householder happiness
hookLine: to Dighajanu: effort, protection, good friends, balanced living

cards: Dighajanu, a layman of the Koliyan people, is honest about his situation. We're householders, he tells the Buddha. We live with wives and children, we use sandalwood, we wear garlands, we handle gold and silver.
Teach us something that will bring us happiness in this life, and in the next. He isn't asking how to leave the world, but how to live in it well.
And the Buddha, whom people sometimes imagine as a teacher of monks only, gives him a plain, practical answer, starting with work and money.

teach.b: For happiness in this life, the Buddha says, four things. First, effort: being skilled and diligent in your work, whether farming, trading, herding or serving the king.

Second, protection: guarding what you've honestly earned, so it isn't lost to theft, fire, flood or careless heirs. Third, good friends: spending time with people who are wise, generous and steady, and learning from them.
Fourth, balanced living, with a picture. A goldsmith or his apprentice holds up a pair of scales and knows: this much has tipped it down, this much has tipped it up.
In the same way, a householder knows what comes in and what goes out, and lives so that income exceeds spending, but not by hoarding. The sutta names both errors.
Live too lavishly, and people say you're eating your wealth like a fig-eater; the old commentary pictures someone shaking a fig tree, knocking most of the fruit to the ground to eat a few.
Live too stingily, and they say you'll die like a starving man.
Then it names four drains on a fortune: chasing other people's spouses, drinking, gambling and bad friends.
And then the other half. For happiness in the next life, four more: faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom, the same four that kept Nakula's parents together.
Money advice and spiritual advice sit in one discourse, side by side, like the two pans of the scale.

how: Buddhist teachers often cite the Dighajanu Sutta, sometimes called the Vyagghapajja Sutta, when speaking about work, money and family life, as the Buddha's counsel for lay people.

o: work, saving, good friends and a balanced budget
enough wealth that you never need to work
a happy home life after leaving the monastery

p: knowing what comes in and goes out

s: the Buddha refused to give advice about money
he gave Dighajanu four practical things for this life, including balanced living.
gambling and drinking are among the four drains on wealth
with chasing others' spouses and bad friends.
the sutta praises saving everything and spending nothing
it warns against both lavishness and stinginess.

games.q: you're a householder with a family and a business. what does the Buddha tell you brings happiness in this life?
o: give away everything and become a monk.
effort, protecting your earnings, good friends, balanced living.
pray for good luck in business.
games.why: four practical things, and then four more for the next life. he answers the householder as a householder.

practice: Picture the goldsmith's scale, two pans and a little needle, and bring to mind one account in your life: money, or time, energy, attention. Read it without judgment, what's coming in, what's going out, which way the needle leans.
Then imagine one small adjustment, a grain added here or taken there, and feel the needle settle toward the middle.

wordCard.voice: Householder happiness. The Buddha's four for this life, effort, protection, good friends and balanced living, and four for the next: faith, virtue, generosity, wisdom. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali samajivikata: 'even living,' balanced living, spending in proportion to income.

carryVoice: Your line: balanced living. Neither the fig-eater nor the starving man. Day six hundred seventy, done.
